report.answer_text:
There isn't one universal definition. It depends on the country, the employer, and the purpose, such as labor law, benefits, or taxes.
United States
The Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA) doesn't define full-time or part-time work. Employers set their own definition, usually 35–40 hours a week.
For the Affordable Care Act (ACA) employer health coverage mandate, full-time means an average of at least 30 hours a week, or 130 hours a month.
The FLSA requires overtime pay at 1.5× for hours over 40 in a workweek for non-exempt employees.
Other countries (typical)
Canada: Usually 30+ hours a week, though it varies by province and employer. Standard weeks are about 40 hours.
UK: There's no statutory definition. Full-time is generally 35–40 hours a week. The Working Time Regulations cap the average week at 48 hours unless the worker opts out.
Australia: The standard full-time week is 38 hours under the National Employment Standards.
France: The legal work week is 35 hours.
Germany: Full-time is typically 35–40 hours, depending on the contract or collective agreement.
Your employer's policy or contract often matters most for benefits eligibility, so check your handbook or contract.
If you tell me your country (and state or province), and whether you're asking about benefits, overtime, or taxes, I can give a more specific answer.
